subtopic: AURORA PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a great deal of interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Chown) in sponsoring second reading of Bill No. S-2, an act to incorporate Aurora Pipe Line Company.
The second reading of a bill is important in parliamentary procedure. It is that phase of procedure where one is expected to and should discuss the principle of the bill, not only the principle of-as in this case-the incorporation of a pipe line company, but all principles allied to the incorporation of the company if it pass through all the procedures of the House of Commons and the other place. In other words, at this stage of second reading it is our responsibility, as members of this house, to consider all the aspects in principle that apply to this bill, as to whether its purport is such as to be in the general interest of Canada or in the particular interest of a phase of the economy of Canada or a part of Canada. We must also relate to its subject matter what it says it is going to do in the solving of a problem which the hon. member for Winnipeg South said has arisen in Alberta.
In other words, it is necessary, not only to consider the actual act of incorporation but to decide on second reading, in principle, whether in relation to its purport and all other factors and previous incorporations this one is in the interests of Canada and of Alberta.
I have no hesitation whatsoever in saying that I feel the second reading of this bill is not something that can be passed over lightly, because its implications are such that very serious consideration must be given by the members of this house to whether it should or should not pass second reading, in the general interests of Canada, the economy of Canada or the particular interest and economy of Alberta.
I am very grateful for the fact that the notice of second reading of this bill was placed on the order paper prior to our adjournment for the Christmas recess. During the course of that recess we were therefore able, with regard to those matters on the order paper of interest to us, to make inquiries and to obtain information. Because I noted on the order paper the second reading of this bill to incorporate Aurora Pipe Line Company I remembered that some two years previously we had incorporated another *company, namely the Foothills Pipe Line Company, for what I think is exactly the :same purpose and to solve the same problem.
[Mr. Chown.)
Therefore I felt-and I am sure that all members will agree-it was necessary, if one had an interest, to obtain the fullest possible information as to why there should be the incorporation now of a new company to serve a purpose obtained by the incorporation of a company some two years ago which was going to meet and fill the same purpose.
So, over the Christmas recess, I sent out inquiries in all directions in order to have the fullest possible information on the purport and principles of this bill and in order to try to find out whether it was one which should pass on second reading in this House of Commons. I am very grateful to all those with whom I communicated for answering the questions I put to them and for supplying me with reports and statements of accounts, information concerning their plans and objectives and so on. After going over all this material I believe the principle of this bill is of such importance that it is incumbent upon me to introduce the entire picture in principle in order that we may have an understanding of the situation and then decide our course of action in this present debate.
Some two years ago, as I mentioned, this house and the other place, after hearing all the reasons and arguments, incorporated a company known as the Foothills Pipe Lines Company. Upon investigation I find that the sponsor of that company was a company known as the Pembina Pipe Line Limited. Thus, I think it is logical that I should start with the Pembina company, deal with its sponsorship of the Foothills company and the reason we incorporated that, and then relate this to the bill now before us. This is what I found.
I found that Pembina Pipe Line Limited is a very large company in western Canada, that the common stock of that company is owned to the extent of approximately 90 per cent by 2,000 Canadian investors with slightly more than 50 per cent of the outstanding shares held by Canadians in the province of Alberta itself. I am informed in writing, and I also have the reports, that as far as Pembina Pipe Line Limited is concerned 95 per cent of all its debt financing has been raised in Canada by Canadian investment houses. It is a company of many years standing which years ago became interested in this problem of the by-products because of gas utilization development in Alberta. Therefore, they employed a number of top notch Canadians to study the problem of these byproducts. The by-products, in the main, are propane, butane, condensate and sulphate and the intention was to see whether there would be a potential market in Canada and, further, if over and above the Canadian market there was a possibility of obtaining an

export market across the international boundary should there be a surplus available.
As a result of their studies, the experts felt -and I quote their own figures and also the figures of Stevenson and Kellogg Limited, a well known firm in Canada who made the analysis for the company-there was a possibility of a $50 million industry in Alberta from the proper collection, transportation, utilization and export of products which were in the main going to waste. When I say $50 million, I mean $50 million annually. Because of this finding, the Pembina Pipe Line Limited sponsored a bill before this house some two years ago to incorporate the Foothills Pipe Lines Company. They did this because of the investigation which has taken place by Canadian scientists and experts and because of the report by Stevenson and Kellogg that it was felt that in western Canada there was a potential utilization of between 20,000 and
40.000	barrels of these liquid gas by-products per day, but that there would still be a surplus of some 70,000 barrels per day.
It was recommended by Stevenson and Kellogg, and in the findings of the Canadian experts, that if it were possible to find a market across the border for those 70,000 barrels, between the utilization of the liquid byproducts in western Canada and across the line, the way would be clear to establish this $50 million a year industry in our country. That was the basis of the request to this house and to the other house for the incorporation of the Foothills Company. That request for incorporation was granted, and all the procedures which the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Chown) said the Aurora Pipe Lines Company are now going through have been undertaken by the Foothills Company and its parent company Pembina Pipe Line Limited. As a result, according to information I received only a short time ago, they have now been able to reach a contractual agreement with Standard Oil in the United States under which the United States company guarantees to take up to 70,000 barrels of these liquid by-products a day in the only place in which they say they can possibly be utilized, that is, in the area of Chicago.
As I pointed out, Pembina Pipe Line Limited is for all purposes Canadian owned and Canadian planned and is the pioneer in this new field. Naturally, some agreement has to be made if you are going to have a company in the United States undertake to receive
75.000	barrels a day compared with the 11,000 barrels mentioned by the hon. member for Winnipeg South which it is felt this new company would be able to export across the line.

Because I knew it would be of vital interest I asked for something official on that and my information is this. As soon as the planned investment now under way comes to fruition the plan calls for Pembina and the Canadian public to own and operate the pipe line facilities in Canada until such time as an export transmission line is built from Alberta to Chicago. This information is under the signature of Pembina. At that time Pembina will sell to Standard three sevenths of its interest in the Alberta facilities. In return, Pembina will purchase 35 per cent of the common stock in all of the United States facilities. On completion of this major transaction the Canadian public will own 30 per cent, Pembina will own 40 per cent, and Standard will own 30 per cent of all the pipe line facilities in Canada. It is estimated that the total project would cost approximately $130 million of which $40 million would be located in Canada.
To initiate the steps required to put such a plant in operation, two years ago Pembina incorporated by special act a company called Foothills Pipe Lines Limited which would be required to transport products across Alberta into the United States. Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company Limited, controlled by the Continental Oil Company of Huston, is now trying to compete with Pembina by offering to take the surplus gas by-products liquids from the extreme south of the province of Alberta into the Continental facilities in the United States. It is my understanding that they have no present intention of extending the Alberta facilities to handle production from gas fields in the north. It is further my understanding that if this contention is correct, then Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company Limited desires to skim off the easy cream of the product at the expense of the other production in the province.
What it is necessary for the House of Commons to know, if such action were permitted through the incorporation of the pipe line company which is now before us, is whether it would imperil the comprehensive and equitable system envisaged by the Pembina Pipe Line Limited and its ancillary company, Foothills Pipeline Limited?
The hon. member for Winnipeg South briefly mentioned the makeup of the company. I am glad he raised that question because if he had not I should have had to. In view of the background of this matter, the potentialities involved and the planning and work that has been done, I simply cannot understand how a Tory could sponsor this bill when one calls to mind the principles expounded with such verbosity by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) in his baby budget relating to Canadian control and Canadian

Private Bills
development of Canadian companies. The minister said the government stands for encouragement and support of the development of resources in Canada by Canadian funds under Canadian control in the utilization of our natural resources. It is difficult to reconcile these two things.
Because this matter intrigued me I made an intensive study of it. We now have before us for second reading a bill designed to do exactly what we said we were going to do when we incorporated two years ago a company which, to the best of my knowledge, has seriously undertaken its responsibilities and forged ahead. We are asked to incorporate a company which suddenly realized the situation and wants to come in perhaps to the detriment of the development of the economy of Alberta and of the disposal of what are now waste products.
As the hon. member for Winnipeg South pointed out, the real sponsor of this bill is the Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company Limited. Hudson's Bay is a famous name in Canada. When we think of it, we think of something Canadian or relating to the United Kingdom. Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company Limited is controlled by a United States company, the Continental Oil Company of Houston. I sent for the last report of Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company Limited on page 14 of which I find that the Continental Oil Company of Houston is said to own 67.8 per cent of the common stock of Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company Limited. The remainder is owned 22.6 per cent by Hudson's Bay Company of England and 9.6 per cent by the United States and Canadian public. In view of the statements of the Prime Minister, (Mr. Diefenbaker), the Minister of Finance and the rank and file backbenchers, it is unmitigated gall to sponsor, introduce and ask us to support the formation of a new company which is 67.8 per cent owned in the United States by the Continental Oil Company of Houston.
We cannot lightly pass over the second reading of this bill. It is of vital concern to us. If the findings of experts and oil engineers are correct, it could mean the development of a $50 million industry in Canada in the utilization of the products and the export of the surplus by-products of gas, propane, butane, sulphur and condensate. As members of this house we have a responsibility to give consideration to whether, in agreeing to the second reading of this bill, we are acting in the best interests of the national economy and of Alberta itself.
I honestly admit that I have an open mind with respect to this bill but as a result of my studies of the records and of the proposals made two years ago and of the work

that has been done since, I question whether we would be doing a favour to Alberta and to Canada by giving second reading to this bill.
I could say a great deal more because of the information I have on my desk, but I say in all sincerity I believe I have been able to give sufficient of the background and of the ramifications behind the introduction of what appears to be a simple bill to incorporate a pipe-line company to draw to the attention of hon. members the importance of the principle and the necessity of a far clearer understanding of what is involved before we give this bill second reading.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a word not so much in rebuttal of the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) but perhaps to try to appeal to logic in so far as procedures are concerned which must be followed in relation to this bill. The hon. member made reference to what was in the best interest of the province of Alberta and Canada as a whole.
When a pipe line company, its sponsors or partners who may be producers, contributors to, or participants in a pipe line company introduce a measure it receives rather close and exacting scrutiny by the provincial authorities. In this instance the scrutiny was given by the Alberta conservation and natural gas board. They make an assessment based on the economic and technical aspects as they affect the jurisdiction or the responsibility of the boards of the provinces. As I say, in this case it was the Alberta conservation and natural gas board.
Then, of course, the sponsors make application to the House of Commons for incorporation. We are at this stage now. If we give this bill second reading it will go to a committee where members will have an opportunity to examine witnesses and discuss various aspects of the proposal. After the bill passes through parliament it will face its most difficult task by going before the national energy board. The responsibilities of the national energy board as we find in the act are to make an assessment similar to that made by the Alberta natural gas and conservation board. As a federal authority its responsibility, of course, is to deal with it from both the technical and economic aspect. After the application is dealt with by the national energy board, and if the application is granted, the company can then proceed to carry out its functions.
I am not suggesting for a moment that the House of Commons does not have a responsibility. Of course we do; but I do point out that by passing this bill we are not in any way losing control over the eventual disposition of the bill itself. First of all, it will go to a committee of the house for

further examination. At this committee witnesses will be called. After the committee makes a report this house will make a searching analysis of the report. I mention this only to point out the procedure through which the bill must go before it becomes law.
The hon. member for Vancouver East made two interesting points, and I am not in entire disagreement with him. But when he talks about the interests of the Dominion of Canada and of the provinces I say to him we must look at the problem that faces Alberta. We can relate this problem to the whole problem of marketing crude oil in its raw state and natural gas or, for that matter, any of the by-products, such as butane, propane, sulphur and condensate.
Reference was made to another pipe-line company which received incorporation in this house. Our problem in Alberta is one of markets. It can be summed up simply in that way. This house is aware of the fact that as far as crude oil is concerned we are able to market less than 50 per cent; the remainder of it is left in the ground. As a result the oil industry finds itself in a difficult position.
I hope to be able to show that if we obtain markets either for our crude product in its basic form or the derivatives from it, it will be to the advantage not only of Alberta but of Canada as a whole. We must keep in mind that the sale of the derivatives of oil may mean a replacement of crude oil. If we can sell these derivatives we will be assisting the general economy within the industry and thus benefiting the province as a whole. I do not think the hon. member will disagree with my last statement because I have discussed it with him personally. The desire to improve the marketing position of the petroleum industry is the general concern of hon. members.
Let us make a comparison of this pipe line company with the one which he has described to us. This pipe line company intends to act as a common carrier. They hope to market a variety of products, derivatives and by-products such as were described by the hon. member, butane, propane, sulphur and condensate.
But what is different is that this company has established for itself through Continental Oil Company a market for one of these byproducts and the important thing is that they have this market. It is not large but it is going to relieve some of the pressure on the rest of the producers in western Canada through the finding of at least this market. He mentioned that the Pembina company had passed through the usual processes of the conservation board. This is not quite accurate.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed consideration of the motion of Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Benidickson.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just before five o'clock I had dealt with what I considered to be the total inadequacy of the hon. members of the opposition in their attempts to deal with this budget and their absolute and dismal failure to come to grips with real, strong issues which are involved in the supplementary budget. I had just started to refer to a statement which had been made by the hon. member for Vancouver East.
I am always glad to listen to the hon. member. He, with two other members of his party -whom it might be embarrassing to name- are what I may call a group within a group. They are hon. members for whom I entertain at certain times certain hopes of salvation. They may well be brands, to be plucked from the burning. But every once in a while while I come to that conclusion they fall from grace with a dull, sickening thud, and yesterday was one of those occasions.
The hon. member had occasion to criticize the hon. member for Carleton and the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway, who in their turn had criticized the text and the tenor of the remarks made by opposition members.
As I understood the hon. member for Vancouver East, he took the position that this government was arrogant and the members who supported the government were not entitled to engage in criticism of this kind. I take exception to that for three reasons. In the first instance I think this is a government


which has always invited and welcomed criticism. It has a capacity for listening to and acting upon valid criticism.
I think a demonstration of that can be found in the debate on the Combines Investigation Act of last year and the Criminal Code amendments which followed it. That was a perfect illustration, and I think there are no such attributes to be found in this government as suggested by the hon. member.
In the second place, when criticism is ill-founded, is unintelligible, is half-baked and is of no value, then I think not only is it a right but it is a duty which falls upon members who support the government to point these things out. Valid, constructive, intelligent criticism is always welcome, and when it does not fall into those categories I think we have a duty to point this out and in turn criticize those who have engaged in that form of argument.
There was a very excellent example of that yesterday when the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway in the course of his remarks had occasion to ask permission of the house to put upon the record certain figures with regard to tax rates which were falling upon individual Canadians. This statement, which I read with some care this morning, places an entirely different light on some of the arguments which were advanced previously by, amongst others, the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson). That is an example of when we are justified in criticizing arguments of this kind.
I think I can give two other illustrations. Last night after I left this house I went home and I was just able to get in on the last part of what I suppose, for want of a better name, might well be called a post mortem on the Liberal rally held during the first three days of last week. I do not know what preceded this particular display, but when I got home Mr. Walter Gordon was being interviewed with regard to this rally and his participation in it.
When I first saw him he was rather happily admitting the suggestion that he had been the grey eminence behind the convention, and with a due modicum of modesty he was brought to admit that in the event this unfortunate country might ever be brought to the state of being inflicted with a Liberal government he would be the next minister of finance.
Having done this, he was then subjected to a very keen and very intelligent line of cross-examination by an interrogator who I believe was Mr. Davey. At this time Mr. Gordon no longer had behind him all the panoply, crowds, display and colour of a rally; he was all by himself and he had the challenge to meet on his own. He was asked1-

and I think this is where he fell down, dismally-to try and reconcile the differences, the deep gulfs which have to be bridged between his line of economic and political thinking, which he had indicated, the future planks of the Liberal platform which had been allowed to see the light of day, and the statements made from time to time by members of the Liberal party in this house. Of course, that is probably an impossible task. He could not do it. It was a complete failure, almost a massacre.
Having in mind that this gentleman, according to his own admission, aspires to be the next minister of finance should there ever be a Liberal government-and I should add, Mr. Speaker, that this is not a paid political advertisement on behalf of the member for Kenora-Rainy River-I think it is proper for members of this party to indulge in criticism of the sort of thing which was displayed there and to do our utmost to see that a Liberal government is not inflicted upon the people of this country.
I think that some time earlier it had been announced that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) had made a statement in which he had challenged the government to bring on an election and had indicated that beyond any doubt, if there was an election he would be successful. I know that is the sort of thing political leaders are supposed to do at rallies of this kind. I have no doubt that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) does not believe it. I have no doubt that no one in this house believes it, but it is the sort of thing the hon. gentleman is expected to do, and he did it.
Unfortunately, there may be a number of people in this country who are not aware of this practice and I can think of nothing more calculated to strike fear and apprehension into the minds of millions of Canadians than the prospect of another Liberal government. Feeling that way, as I do, I am sure that along with many hon. members on this side I am entitled by my actions and speeches here to see, along with my colleagues, that this is not brought about.
It is not only the actions and program of the government which are at issue. We must also consider, under our democratic system, the programs of those political parties which hope to offer an alternative, the character of the leaders of those parties and their ability to implement the programs which are proposed. For these reasons I take strong issue with what was said by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) and when necessary I intend to continue to criticize the type
The Budget-Mr. Baldwin of specious argument which has been developed ad nauseam during this debate on the opposition side.
It would be all very well for me to say to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) that this is a good budget and an opportune budget brought down at the right time and containing the right material, but I can go outside my own thoughts and outside the opinions of those who support the Minister of Finance. I have here the annual review section of Montreal Gazette of January 14. The leading article is written by Mr. John A. Meyer who, I think, is a reasonable, intelligent and well qualified observer in the field of political economy and one who, I think, takes an independent attitude. The headlines above this article read:
Nation on new tack. An economy shaped to national aspirations. Aim is sufficient independence, diversity and strength for maintenance of a political sovereignty.
I should like to read a few of the paragraphs from this very interesting article:
The Canadian economy never before was subjected to such searching scrutiny as during 1960. The process will continue through 1961. The supplementary budget was a first indication of new directions. The main budget should be even more definitive. A deliberate effort is now being tnade to shape an economy compatible with national needs and national aspirations. The process, in Canadian tradition, will be slow- evolutionary rather than revolutionary. All that really can be said so far is that a start has been made; with so much yet to be done the going now will not necessarily be easier.
The article continues:
The results of several enquiries now under way should be available by budget time. The government should be able to implement, with the certainty of thorough prior and public examination, findings on operation of the railroads, on conduct of the automobile industry, the periodical press and the coal industry. It will have the initial results of the Senate enquiry into unemployment. Most important of all, it will have the experience of the supplementary budget to draw upon in the preparation of new measures.
There are other items I should like to deal with, but time will not permit. However, there is just one statement I should like to extract from its context and read:
If the government's actions now appear to be extreme, it is because, in large part, so much is now being done which should have been done before.
That is a point to which I shall return, Mr. Speaker. This not only lends comfort to the Minister of Finance in connection with the bringing down of this budget and the legislation proposed to complement it, but I think it constitutes by implication a strong rebuke to those members of the opposition parties who have engaged in the form of criticism of this budget to which I have referred.

The Budget-Mr. Baldwin
I wish in particular to comment on a television appearance made, I think, in a program called "The Nation's Business" by the Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer) on the eve of the national rally. I do not remember all that was said, and I did not catch it all, but one statement was made-I do not know which of the two hon. gentlemen made it- containing strong criticism of this budget and the related actions of the government on the ground that it was nothing but a long range program.
In the first place, I reject the suggestion that there are no short range programs of immediate value connected with this budget. If necessary, I could turn to this very authentic document which was branded by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) and which is known as "The Record Speaks" from which the hon. gentleman quoted. I think that having quoted from it he should have gone on to put it on record in Hansard for the edification of the people of Canada.
This is an accurate account, illustrated by chapter and verse with reference to the statutes of this country, indicating what steps have been taken by this government to increase the economic standards and the wellbeing and welfare of the people of this country. I could go outside this document. In the article to which I referred by Mr. Meyer, and in the articles following it, we find a number of expressions of opinion by various people in different areas of the political and economic life of this country. We find on page 4 of this supplement, for example-and I recommend the reading of this to all hon. members before they engage in further criticism-an article by Mr. H. W. Thomson, president of the Canadian Bankers' Association. Among other things, he said this:
Additional deposit accounts were opened at a rate of more than 2,000 every banking day during the 12-month period ending September 30, 1960. Personal savings accounts increased by 384,358 and other deposit accounts of the public by 156,780 making a total number of accounts at September 30 of 12,713,000. In the past 10 years they have increased by more than 50 per cent.
At September 30, 1960, personal savings in the chartered banks stood at $7,310 million, $71 million higher than the year before and the highest figure on record.
I turn also to a statement from a publication cited by the hon. member for Vancouver -Kingsway (Mr. Browne) last night and referred to as "Industry". In the same article which, I think, he mentioned is the statement:
How many of us, for instance, know that there are 250,000-one quarter of a million-more Canadians with jobs today than there were three years ago.

I think that constitutes an ample answer to those who say there are no short range characteristics of immediate benefit to this country in the government's program. It is my submission-and I submit this with confidence-that the long range programs envisaged in this budget and complemented by the legislation and planned action of the government are something we should have had many years ago long before the Liberal government was thrown out of office in 1957.
The period of gestation of many of the economic movements in a country like ours today is of long duration and the fruits we harvest at present are in many instances the result of seeds sown years ago. That has been a fatal error into which the former Liberal government fell. For that reason I think it ill behooves them to criticize the budget and the other measures introduced by this government because they show, in effect, long range planning. Three of those steps to which I will refer speak eloquently of the values and virtues that will stem from them.
The intention clearly indicated in the budget of enabling Canadians to enjoy a greater measure of participation in the development of their own natural resources and a greater share in their ownership is something which should have been commenced eight or ten years ago when it was fully apparent that a dangerous situation was going to come about because of what was happening with regard to the ownership of our natural resources.
One of the important measures to which I referred is the question of trade expansion under which additional financial guarantees to exporters will be implemented.
A second is the imaginative mass meeting held at the instigation of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees) under which trade commissioners from various parts of the world and thousands upon thousands of Canadian businessmen were brought together. This has already had a favourable impact. A few days ago I spoke to a person I regard as an informed observer of the economic picture who had just returned from Europe and the United Kingdom. His unequivocal statement to me was that there has already been as a result of this program a most beneficial impact upon the European and United Kingdom political and economic scene.
Finally there is the inquiry instigated by this government in the other place by a special committee of the problems of manpower and the related and integrated effect so far as unemployment is concerned and the direction our economy should take.
These are steps which should have been foreseen as being required eight, 10 or 12 years ago but I suppose it would be too much

to suggest that a government and party whose trademark was procrastination and delay, a party of day to day expediency and bits and pieces legislation, who were never comfortable when they had to take a stand and if they could not find a fence available when a decision had to be made would build one to sit on, would be the sort of government or party one would reasonably expect to launch measures of this kind.
Under the present administration these and other forward looking measures will, I suggest, take the people of this country far ahead in their search for prosperity and happiness.

Some of the means set forth in the budget are double depreciation for industry, the extension of the 21 per cent tax on corporate profits from the $25,000 bracket to the $35,000 bracket, Canadian income restrictions on investment corporations and pension trusts, the repeal of the 4 per cent surtax on income from Canadian investment, the increase on the withholding tax from 5 to 15 per cent and the tax penalties on bonds owned outside of Canada by non-residents. All these sound very imposing, but when we come to analyse them we find they are not so effective as one might be led to expect.
Take for example the question of double depreciation. We in the Atlantic provinces are keenly interested in this measure because it is specifically designed to attract industry into underdeveloped areas where there is a high level of unemployment. When we come to examine this measure we find it is applicable for only one year and it is hedged around with so many conditions that it is unlikely that many companies will be induced to bother with it at all. Even if a company does take advantage of it, what is gained in the one year is likely to be lost later on by a reduction in capital cost book value. Therefore, actually this measure is not really a tax deduction but a tax postponement, and that is a great disappointment to those of us who are interested in the development of our resources in the maritime provinces. If this is the best that the government can offer- and it is the only thing in this budget-then

The Budget-Mr. Carter we may as well forget about it because it falls so very far short of what is required.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The extension of the 21 per cent tax on profits from the $25,000 bracket to the $35,000 bracket will be a welcome tax reduction to those small businesses whose profits fall between these two figures, but it will be no help at all to the vast numbers of small enterprises whose taxable profits fall below $25,000.
Small business enterprises are the backbone of our economy, and if we are to make an all out attack on unemployment this, in my opinion, is one of the best ways of doing it because there are so many small businesses that if we can enable them to employ only one extra member on their staff, by the sheer force of their numbers alone they will make a considerable contribution toward solving the unemployment problem. If we add to them the people who would be employed indirectly by the enlargement of their premises and by additions to their equipment, then we can see that small businesses can make a very important contribution toward creating the jobs that we need if we are to come to grips with this unemployment problem. But to do that we must consider all the small business people who should receive some measure of tax assistance, and not merely those whose profits happen to fall between $25,000 and $35,000.
Restrictions on the pension trusts and on investment houses themselves cannot have very much positive effect on our problem because most of those companies or organizations already have a sufficient proportion of Canadian securities in their portfolios to enable them to comply with the law without increasing them. What we actually need is a more direct incentive which would pay the investor to buy common and preferred stock rather than bonds and mortgages.
The repeal of the 4 per cent surtax on Canadian investment income will help a
[Mr. Carter.)

number of individuals, widows and older people who are dependent on investment income, but it cannot be expected to exert any appreciable influence on the flow of equity funds.
The increase in the withholding taxes illustrates a new feature which is characteristic of the Conservative party, and that is its accent on Canadian nationalism. While it may sound patriotic, we know that forces are at work, ready and eager to exploit this emphasis in such a way as to generate anti-Americanism, and some of those overtones are already audible. The record of the Conservative party is not to be envied in this respect. My hon. friends remember their references to the Texas buccaneers when they were sitting over here in opposition, and they remember their references to the IS per cent trade diversion and the tough line that they were going to take with the U.S.A., all of which were planks in their election platform. They also remember their truculent reaction to the feelings of the people of the United States which arose in relation to the recent Cuban trade overtures, and now these measures emphasizing economic nationalism with their unfortunate overtones of anti-Americanism.
The United States investor can hardly be blamed if he gets the idea that his risk capital is not welcome here in Canada. The fact is that Canada cannot do without United States venture capital. We have somewhere around 500,000 people unemployed at the present time. Within six months time, after schools are out, around July or August, there will be another 200,000 additional people in the working force looking for jobs. Where are all those jobs to come from? They can come only from the investment of venture capital.
Someone in the United States has calculated that it requires $10,000 of capital to create one job, and I presume that the figure is pretty much the same for Canada. Canada simply has not enough capital to create all those jobs, and furthermore Canadians are not willing to invest what capital they have; otherwise, what would be the necessity for all these special inducements outlined in the budget?
I ask my hon. friends, where would Newfoundland be today but for the investment of United States capital? How much Canadian capital has been invested in my province since we became part of Canada in 1949? It is so trivial that it is too insignificant to mention, and that has been one of our greatest disappointments about confederation.
The United States can hardly be blamed if it feels that it is not obliged to continue the special consideration which we have enjoyed heretofore. A short time ago the Pentagon in the United States sent out orders to its armed

forces to restrict spending on purchases for United States troops abroad. As a special consideration Canada was exempted from that order, and that meant a lot to many communities in my province whose economies are tied in with the existence of United States bases.
In Newfoundland our fresh and frozen fish industry is completely dependent upon the United States market. On several occasions the fish lobbies in the United States having made representations to their government and to special committees set up for the purpose have succeeded in getting recommendations put through which would place restrictions upon imports of our fresh fish products. That was overcome on two occasions only by a presidential veto. If such a situation arises in the future the President of the United States would hardly, in my opinion, feel himself obliged to come to our rescue again and if he does not it is going to be very disastrous for my province.
Let us not forget too that the United States is the bulwark of our freedom. Canada is a part of the free world and the United States is the leader of that free world. The main policy of the Kremlin today is to divide Canada from the United States and to stir up disunity between our peoples. Anything that contributes to that disunity endangers the security, not only of Canada but also of the whole free world.
There were two other notable omissions in this budget which in my opinion should cause some concern. One is that there was no indication of coming to grips with the underlying causes of our economic trouble and the other is that there was no recognition of any need for a change in our financial machinery. One of the major causes of our financial troubles today is that the fiscal policy of the government and the monetary policy of the Bank of Canada are not in harmony and, in fact, they have been out of step ever since this government took office.
This raises the question of over-all responsibility. It is true that the Bank of Canada is charged under the Bank of Canada Act with the responsibility of maintaining the stability of our Canadian currency but since our dollar was freed on the international exchange its value has been at a premium abroad while at the same time it has depreciated in value at home by an average of about 2 per cent per year for the past 20 years. That suggests that perhaps we are saddling the Bank of Canada with a responsibility which it is impossible to discharge.
When the fiscal policy of the government and the monetary policy of the Bank of Canada were in close harmony, as they were
The Budget-Mr. Carter under the Liberal regime, there was positive leadership and direction which could be easily recognized by the business community, but when they are out of step, as they have been for some time now, confusion and chaos result. Since the monetary policy of the bank is subject to a large extent to the direct influence of the fiscal policy of the government, it is logical that the over-all responsibility should rest with the government and the Minister of Finance would do a lot to clear up the present confusion if he would plainly accept that responsibility.
A second major cause of our economic troubles is the fact that our financial machinery is out of date. Our present system is some 25 or 30 years old and during that time tremendous and fundamental changes have taken place in our economic life but there has been no change at all in our financial machinery. As a Liberal I believe in individual freedom. I believe an individual should be free to do what he wants provided he keeps within the law and does not restrict the freedom of anyone else. Above all, the individual should be free to meet the needs of his fellow men. But we are not free to do so. We may see needs around us, we may have the resources and the will to take care of them but we are not free to go ahead and do it.
The system or somebody behind the system determines what needs are going to be met and who is going to meet them. A young couple may wish to own a home of their own. The home may be worth around $15,000. They can find the $15,000 to lay out for the value of the house but they are not free to acquire that house because the system, in addition to the $15,000 for the house, requires them to pay another $15,000 in interest which they certainly cannot afford.
The fundamental problem facing Canadians today is to maintain and expand our standard of living in a changing world. Our financial system is one of the means by which this is to be achieved. But experience has proved that only on very rare occasions when very special conditions have happened to exist at the same time have we been able to enjoy prosperity without inflation. For the greater part of that time the system has operated so as to compel us to choose between two evils, inflation on the one hand and unemployment on the other.
The primary reason for the existence of our financial, industrial and commercial organizations is to meet the needs of the people. In Canada we have a vast reservoir of human needs crying out to be met, not to speak of the vast abundance of human needs elsewhere. Here in Canada we also have an abundance of natural resources, of materials,

The Budget-Mr. Carter skills and industrial capacity, a great part of which is now lying idle. Moreover, we have a huge surplus of manpower of somewhere around 500,000 people.
Surely a financial system adequate to present day conditions would function in such a way as to bring all these elements together and to act as a catalyst so that the industrial machine can start turning over to fulfil its primary function of meeting the needs of mankind. The fact that our industrial machine is slowing down and a large section of it has already come to a standstill, while at the same time we have approximately half a million out of work with millions of needs waiting to be filled, is in itself sufficient proof that our present financial system is no longer adequate.
In addition, no new production or at best very little can come into existence today without generating a corresponding burden of debt and more and more it is becoming the case that new production cannot be consumed without incurring an additional debt burden, so much so that many of our workers today have mortgaged a large part of their earnings for two or three years in advance. How long can this be expected to continue? Surely it is bound to catch up with us some day sooner or later and when it does the effects are likely to be disastrous.
Mr. Coyne has told us on a number of occasions that we are living beyond our means. Mr. Coyne's statements would be much more helpful if he would be more precise in defining his terms and exactly what he has in mind when he refers to "our means". If by "our means" he means our capacity to incur additional debt, then I think we must agree with him because it seems to me that there is something immoral about taking the easy way out by incurring a debt burden which we are going to pass on to the next generation, particularly if they are not going to derive any benefit from it. The next generation will have enough to do to cope with their own problems without inheriting problems from us. Mr. Coyne's statement, as does this budget, appears to be based on two assumptions.
One of these assumptions is that there is no alternative to the present system, and the other assumption is that the present system cannot be improved; that we are stuck with it and we must continue to live with it and adjust ourselves to it whenever necessary for all time to come.
Now, these two assumptions I, for one, am not prepared to accept, at least not with the information that has been made available to date. In my opinion, it is absurd that man can put a sputnik into orbit and guided mis-

siles into space, yet he has not the ingenuity to correct these obvious defects in our financial system or replace it with one that is even better. What should be done? Obviously, the first step is to find out where our financial machinery has broken down. I, for this reason, urge the government once again as I have already done on several occasions to set up a royal commission or some appropriate body to completely investigate and examine our financial system and to recommend what changes should be made to correct its obvious defects and inadequacies.

We are the party of the people, and the voice of the people is our strength. One of the reasons why the Canadian people decided to end the Liberal reign was that the former government became aloof from the people. I have heard Liberal backbenchers say they could hardly get appointments with ministers at the end of those long 22 years. The present ministers were out and about this country. The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) was out and about this country. Members of parliament belonging to this party are going about their constituencies, because we have the intention of keeping in touch with the people. We know our mandate comes from the people of Canada, and unlike those who for so long behaved in a cool, quasi-intellectual way, we are going to keep in touch with the people. We are the party of the people and we understand what the aspirations and desires of all Canadians are.
Members opposite have criticized this government by saying its policies contain a high degree of nationalism. They say we are going to lose friends abroad. Let me briefly read some remarks which I have penned, with a friend of mine, in relation to the present budget.
The federal budget, like the early legislation which has been introduced at the present session, gives the impression of having been well conceived and planned. Regarding this spirit of nationalism of which some hon. members have made mention, I say the government's position is made clear in two paragraphs of the speech made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming). I should like to quote those two paragraphs because I think they are of primary importance:
It has sometimes been asserted that the participation of foreigners in Canadian business and in our capital markets should no longer be welcome and that investment from abroad should be sharply curtailed by policies directed to this end. This is not the view of this government. The result of blocking out foreign investors and foreign investment would be to produce a "little Canada", cut off from many of the contacts with the outside world that have enriched our national life. We would become comparatively isolated, and most of us would be disappointed by the effects of our economic development.
The minister went on to say:
As I have already made clear in this speech, and frequently on other occasions, it is my view that the Canadian economy has derived great benefits from the inflow of capital from abroad and benefits still continue to accrue. Our national development has been accelerated thereby; the breadth and depth of our industrial structure have been increased; the scope of productive occupations for our own citizens has been extended. There is no intention therefore of recommending policies antagonistic to foreign capital. To do so would not be in the best interests of Canada.
I think these two paragraphs must be underlined and borne in mind during this debate. They must be borne in mind by those who in an irresponsible fashion would like to pretend that this supplementary budget has undertones or overtones of narrow nationalism in it.
I should now like very briefly to discuss what are, in my opinion, some of the more important technical enactments contained in this supplementary budget.
The imposition of a 15 per cent withholding tax on the interest of federal and provincial government bonds represents one important legislative change. Federal government issues were previously exempt and provincial issues subject to 5 per cent. This action will deter the non-resident buying of treasury bills and short term government

securities to take advantage of discrepancies in interest rates in the international money-market. It thereby provides the Bank of Canada with freer action in monetary policy without being concerned that the action that should be taken would contribute to a strengthening of the false premium on the Canadian dollar.
Second, incentives earlier were introduced to enable provincial and municipal governments to finance in the New York market. In order to obtain a good reception to such issues legislation was introduced that such issues in United States funds would not be subject to the withholding tax applicable to other non-residents in the payment of Canadian dividends and interest. It is broadly accepted that it is no longer as desirable to have provincial and municipal governments financing in New York, in part because of our already high deficit in international payments-and in part because it adds to the false premium strength of the Canadian dollar. The reasoning is soundly based and it thereby makes sense to eliminate the incentive and to make the financing, regardless as to where it takes place, subject to a 15 per cent withholding tax when the interest and dividends are paid to a non-resident.
Thus the application of the 15 per cent withholding tax on the dividends of wholly owned non-resident subsidiaries only removes an inequity and makes the factors equal for all non-resident investors earning an investment income from the Canadian economy. The United States investment withholding tax with countries with which it does not have a reciprocal tax agreement, such as France, Switzerland, the Philippines and many others is 30 per cent.
A third thing I should like to mention is that the change in the customs tariff is complex but without transgressing the agreement of GATT. It gives the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) discretional authority to more effectively rule with respect to the provisions of section 6 of the Customs Tariff containing the anti-dumping clause which applies only to goods of a class or kind made or produced in Canada. It deals with a qualification of this last clause and defines class or kind more specifically and eliminates the loopholes under which small modifications are made and under which it is then claimed such goods are not produced in Canada. The new resolution proposes that in the case of goods custom-made to specifications they should be deemed to be of a class or kind made or produced in Canada if adequate facilities exist in Canada for the economic production of such goods within a reasonable period of time. It is further provided that goods shall be

deemed to be of a class or kind made or produced in Canada if goods of approximately the same class or kind are made or produced in Canada. The change strengthens the antidumping clauses in the tariff structure.
I think these facts should be tabled at the present time to clarify general understanding in relation to the intentions of this supplementary budget.
The supplementary budget enacted tax considerations for those individuals who have children at universities. This enactment, coupled with the present government's attitude toward vocational schools in cooperation with the municipalities, underlies the real importance of education in our contemporary society.

My topic this evening will be wrong-doing, wickedness and water and I shall relate those three words to the discussion of a subject which to some extent comes within the jurisdiction of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming). I am pleased that the perceptive, patient, perambulating parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Bell) is in his seat. I wish to mention first of all the question of the repeated failures of small United States lumber companies in the interior of British Columbia whose owners and operators after bankruptcy disappear across the United States border. I have been asked to mention this by a large number of the persons affected. I bring it to the attention of the Minister of Finance in the hope that the situation will be reviewed to see if amendments can be made to the Bankruptcy Act to cover up what appear to be present loopholes and to see if some legislation can be introduced to protect the interests of Canadian working people and other Canadian creditors.
The most recent case brought to my attention is the failure of the Hilco Lumber Company, near Fruitvale, British Columbia. I attended a creditors' meeting. This is not my responsibility but my constituents have considerable confidence in my advice and in my willingness to do what I can to assist. I attended this meeting of about 100 people. There were present some 60 workingmen who had been employed for several months by this company. In addition there were storekeepers and other creditors. Some of the workingmen were owed as much as $900. They had been asked to continue working without pay from month to month. The scamps gave them some cheques and disappeared across the border. The lumber, of course, had gone across to the United States. These employees were left without anything in the nature of reimbursement for their services. Storekeepers, oil companies and other suppliers were left without payment for their goods. It was brought to my attention at the meeting that the company had collected income tax from the employees over a period of two years. Approximately $14,000 is owing to the income tax department.
When the employees went to the unemployment insurance office it was found the company had not purchased unemployment insurance stamps. There is some laxity in this respect and checking required for the protection of the workers involved.

This company goes broke owing over half a million dollars. About $19,000 is due to the workers by way of wages. Many local businessmen are creditors. Federal and provincial governments are creditors, as I mentioned.
During the last 18 months about 12 million board feet of lumber was taken from the woods, most of same consisting of tamarae, cedar, fir, hemlock and balsam and was shipped to the Hill Lumber Company, also owned by Mr. Pidge, at Curlew, Washington.
Small shipments were made to other companies in Canada.
An unknown number of cheques have been issued which are in excess of the $19,000. They were issued to pay workers, subcontractors and creditors. Many have been returned in an insufficient funds condition. Some have been passed into local businesses which are unable to claim money from the men.
A study of accounts payable would indicate that moneys are owing to the federal and provincial governments. It is believed that seizure proceedings have been taken of the rough lumber remaining.
1 bring this matter to the attention of the parliamentary secretary on behalf of these unfortunate people in the hope that consideration will be given to them. This is only one instance. I am informed that this rascal has done this twice before. I am informed he also operates lumber companies in the United States;
It seems to me there is a need for legislation that would protect Canadian citizens under these circumstances. It is the same old story. Wages are left unpaid; the operator ships the last 12 million feet of lumber across the line and disappears with it, telling the men that he will be back on Monday to pay their wages.
This is happening repeatedly. On this account, because of its recurrence and the unnecessary hardship that it creates, I do suggest that the government give consideration to amending the Bankruptcy Act. I say that because first of all the company went into voluntary liquidation. Then the creditors began to realize that voluntary liquidation might mean administration over a long period and there would not be much left for them, and they attempted to enter a petition of

bankruptcy. The creditors informed me that they could find no one on whom to serve a summons of petition of bankruptcy; there was no local agent, no officer and no office. There must be a loophole there. With respect to the Bankruptcy Act, some consideration should be given to amending it to prevent this type of thing happening, if it is at all possible. In addition to that, I suggest that possibly there could be some legislation which would require persons operating under those circumstances, who are not Canadian citizens, and who are obviously able to disappear overnight, to post some bond or something else with some provincial or federal authority to assure the payment of income tax, unemployment insurance tax, provincial taxes, wages and so on.
I have dealt with the case rather briefly, but I promised my constituents that I would bring this matter to the attention of the house and the minister, and I do urge that this problem be given some consideration.
In the few minutes time remaining to me, Mr. Speaker, I am going to speak about the proposed development on the Columbia river. I am not going to deal with the issue at stake, whether this is good or that is good, but I have been asked by those opposed to the high Arrow dam in my district to mention this in the house and to give the house some idea of the organized opposition. When hon. members receive literature, as they will from now on from this committee, and possibly have representations made to the caucuses of the various parties, and the government and others receive representations they will understand the well organized opposition that exists. This protest arises out of the building of the high Arrow dam. I am not going into that except to indicate that it means the destruction of 18 communities and the flooding of 40,000 acres of forest and agricultural land and the displacement of 1,700 people, the most of whom have nowhere to go because the water will come up the mountainside.
I have seen references in the press to the fact that I am the owner of property that might be flooded. This is incorrect. My wife is the owner of the property; I live there under sufferance. We are more fortunate than others. We are losing a beautiful beach and besides that we shall probably lose a log cabin. However we can move back a thousand feet or so and rebuild, but many people cannot. Their beaches will be destroyed, their orchards, their fields, their houses and so on. In addition to that, the whole of the industrial area of Revelstoke will be flooded and destroyed. Nothing will be left but the upper town if this flooding occurs. The lumber mills, the pole yards,

I want to thank the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Brunsden) for his assistance in proving that I am even more in order than I thought I was. I wish to bring to the attention of members of the house the people who are involved in this organization. The organizations who are opposed not to the development of the Mica creek dam or the development suggested by General McNaughton but to this high Arrow dam are: the chambers of commerce of Revelstoke, Nakusp, lower Arrow lakes, Castlegar and Nelson, the city council of Revelstoke, the mine, mill and smelter workers union of British Columbia, the B.C. federation of labour, the B.C. auto courts and resorts association, the west Kootenay farmers' institute, the west Kootenay's women's institute-God bless the women- the Arrow boat club of Castlegar, the Nakusp launch club, the Nakusp livestock breeders' association and numerous other local organizations. You can see that there is solid foundation of people from all walks of life, business, labour and farmers.
These people have met and have elected what is known as the Arrow lakes and Revelstoke city water resources committee. The members of the committee were elected to represent these groups and the people for the purpose of making representations to the federal and provincial governments, and I am very glad to hear that they will have the opportunity to make representations to the external affairs committee of this house.
They have secured as their engineering consultant Mr. F. J. Bartholomew, a consulting electrical engineer of Vancouver who has had a lot of experience with hydro developments and construction. In addition, they have Mr. Boyd Affleck, an engineer from Nelson, B.C., and the assistance of quite a number of other engineers who are turning up from all sorts of places and who are willing to assist in the preparation of briefs some of whom have also indicated that they are willing to come to Ottawa with Mr. 
Bartholomew and others to explain their views and give their opinions before the external affairs committee.
I might say at this time that the committee is raising money and it is surprising how concerned and interested people are. They are collecting funds. They have collected nearly $1,000 on the Arrow lakes and the city of Revelstoke is now collecting funds. The people are behind this movement. I happened to visit Revelstoke on the way to Ottawa and addressed a public meeting at the invitation of the chamber of commerce at which members of the municipal council, the chamber of commerce and the public were present. They were representative of all political parties and I never saw a group of people in a city so solidly behind a movement no matter what their party politics are. Once this flooding happens the economic life of the city of Revelstoke will disappear with the exception of the trade from a declining number of C.P.R. employees who stop off there between trains because the divisional points are now Vancouver and Calgary.
To illustrate the interest in the campaign I might say that on Christmas morning a pioneer rancher on the upper Arrow lakes by the name of John Nelson telephoned me and said, "I want to tell you that I was up until Christmas day posting literature on the Galena bay wharf opposing the high Arrow dam and I am sending a cheque for $100". That is the way it is up and down the lakes. If hon. members know of anyone who is willing to subscribe to the fund for the campaign against the destruction of the natural resources of the Arrow lakes, tell them to write to the secretary of the water resources committee, Nakusp, B.C., or the secretary of the committee of the chamber of commerce of Revelstoke. They would be very pleased to receive donations. I may say we have had donations from the Okanagan and from some persons on the coast who are interested in this matter.
Literature is being printed and distributed to members of parliament and members of the provincial house. I urge you to read this literature so that you will have some understanding of this most difficult problem. It is a difficult problem to understand thoroughly unless one lives in the area. I have travelled in Indian canoes on the Columbia. No member of the house knows more about the Columbia than I do, not because I am a wiser person but because I happen to have lived there the greater part of my life. I know the circumstances, I know the depth of water in all the different channels, where the bays are and the dam sites will be and that sort of thing. I should know that because I have lived there. I ask members to study this

literature and get some grasp of the attitude of these people in the district which I have the honour to represent because their attitude is completely non-partisan and Canadian.
As a matter of fact, if my own party supported the high Arrow dam I would vote against it but thank goodness my party stands for the preservation of our natural resources and is opposed to any unnecessary destruction of the same. Now, Mr. Speaker, I will say in reply to the hon. member for-

In the few minutes that are left before ten o'clock there is one point I should like to make.^ During this debate we are actually speaking on the budget and on the amendment which was made. Several questions have been asked, and several times the same question has been asked, why did the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) bring down a budget at this time and what good did it do? There is one thing that a budget at this time did, Mr. Speaker, and I think it deserves the commendation of everyone. While the Canadian trade balance has been adverse, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees) has made tremendous efforts to increase our trade.
One of the most difficult things that we have had to meet has been the currency exchange rate. The fact that the Canadian dollar has been high in relation to the United States dollar has been one of the difficulties facing our exporters. It has caused a great deal of trouble. As a result of the announcement made by the Minister of Finance in the budget, the dollar has very nearly reached par. At the moment there is only a difference of five eighths of one per cent between the

Business of the House
Canadian and the United States dollar. This makes it very much easier for the exporter to sell his products outside Canada at a price which will compete with goods offered in other countries.
Then, too, the achievement of near parity with the United States dollar will be of great assistance to the people in the tourist and catering industries in this country. This has always been one of the things to be met when United States visitors came to Canada. There may be only a few cents difference and the visitors do not mind paying. However, in Canada we have those people who will collect the odd few cents, and in some cases this is necessary, but in so doing they lose a great deal of trade. This achievement of near parity with the United States dollar will do a great deal for our tourist industry and our catering industry during the coming season. We hope that the dollar will remain at par or very close to it. If it does, I am sure it will be a great spur both to our tourist industry and to our exporters in this country.
I have other remarks to make, Mr. Speaker, and I have a plan to evolve arising out of the budget, the speech from the throne and the items of legislation that the government proposes. When this debate resumes 1 should like to deal with these subjects in greater detail, but I should like now to call it ten o'clock.
